text:
One of the most persistent myths about science is that research is, or once was, or ought to be, untouched by money. The facts are these: companies pay for research because they want new products to sell, and governments pay for it because they want to meet national needs such as health and defence. Science has always gone where the funding goes.
Which one of the following is a conclusion that can be drawn from the above passage?
options: Scientists secretly admit that their research is shaped by its funders.
Showing that research follows the money only exposes as a myth the idea that science is free of money.
Companies should not be allowed to pay for research.
Governments should pay for all research.
solution: The passage calls science free of money a myth and gives the facts of who pays and why. So pointing out that funding shapes research reveals nothing scandalous: it only exposes that myth. The passage makes no claim about what scientists admit, does not say money ruins science, and proposes no rules about who should fund it.

text:
Twelve riders took part in a six-stage cycling race. In each stage the first five finishers scored points: 1st 10, 2nd 6, 3rd 4, 4th 2, 5th 1.
Every rider finished in the top three at least once, but only Lena, the overall winner with 46 points, finished in the top three in every stage.
How many stages did Lena win?
solution: Lena's six results were all 1st, 2nd or 3rd. If she won w stages and came 2nd in s, then 10w + 6s + 4(6 - w - s) = 46, which simplifies to 3w + s = 11. With w + s at most 6, the only solution is w = 3, s = 2 (and one 3rd place): 30 + 12 + 4 = 46. The other riders' results do not change this.

text:
Tom makes wooden toys. The materials for one toy cost €2.40, and he pays his assistant €12 an hour. A wooden train takes the assistant 40 minutes to make. Tom sells each toy for 50% more than it costs him to produce.
What is the selling price of one wooden train?
solution: Labour for 40 minutes is two-thirds of €12, which is €8.00, so the train costs €2.40 + €8.00 = €10.40 to make. Adding 50% gives €10.40 x 1.5 = €15.60. Adding the markup only to the materials gives €11.60, and charging a full hour of labour leads to €21.60.

text:
Health officials are worried that doctors do not wash their hands often enough between patients. The plan is to start by training medical students in strict hand-washing routines, so that, as they qualify and become senior, good habits spread upwards until the whole profession is improved.
Which one of the following, if true, would most weaken this plan?
options: Medical students spend little time on hospital wards.
Hand-washing posters have been on hospital walls for years.
Hand gel is quicker to use than soap and water.
Medical students are more willing to follow rules than qualified doctors.
Most doctors working in the country's hospitals trained abroad.
solution: The plan relies on today's students becoming tomorrow's doctors, so that the habits spread from the bottom up. If most hospital doctors trained abroad, the students trained here will be only a small part of the profession, and the plan cannot improve the whole of it. Students' willingness to follow rules, if anything, supports the plan.

text:
Lucia packs boxes in a warehouse from Monday to Friday. She must pack at least 100 boxes every working day, and she earns a basic wage of €300 a week plus a bonus of €2 for every box above 120 that she packs on any single day.
Last week she earned €420 in total. On Wednesday she packed 150 boxes, more than on any other day she has ever worked.
What is the smallest number of boxes she could have packed last week?
solution: The bonus was €120, so 60 boxes were above the 120 mark. Wednesday gives 30 of them. The other 30 must come from other days, but no other day reached 150, so no single day can supply all 30: at least two more days carry the extra, for example 149 and 121. Those three days total 150 + 270 = 420, and the last two days need only the minimum 100 each: 620.

text:
A table-tennis league is played over 5 rounds. In each round the winner scores 2 points and the runner-up 1 point; the league goes to the player with most points.
The players are Ana, Bea, Cleo and Dora. Each of them won at least one round. In every round the runner-up was Bea or Cleo. No winner and runner-up pairing happened twice, and Dora never won a round in which Bea was the runner-up.
Who won the league?
solution: With Bea or Cleo always second, the possible (winner, runner-up) pairs are Ana-Bea, Ana-Cleo, Bea-Cleo, Cleo-Bea, Dora-Cleo (Dora-Bea is ruled out). That is exactly five different pairings for five rounds, so each happened once. Points: Ana 2 + 2 = 4; Bea 2 + 1 + 1 = 4; Cleo 2 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 5; Dora 2. Cleo won.

text:
Some cities now require restaurants to print the number of calories next to every dish on the menu. A review concluded that these labels are a cheap and effective way to help people eat fewer calories. All countries should therefore make calorie labels compulsory.
Which one of the following, if true, most weakens this argument?
options: People who are overweight face higher health risks.
In the cities that introduced labels, a tax on sugary drinks and a healthy-eating campaign in schools began at the same time.
Restaurants earn more from high-calorie dishes.
Another country is planning to introduce menu labels.
solution: If other measures started at the same time, the fall in calories may be due to them rather than the labels, so the review's conclusion, and the recommendation built on it, is less secure. Memorable information and health risks support labelling, restaurant profits do not bear on whether labels work, and another country's plan is not evidence.

text:
Nina walked a long-distance trail over 8 days.
On day 1 she walked 12 km, and on days 2 and 3 she walked 25 km each; by the end of day 4 she had completed exactly 40% of the trail. She walked 27 km on each of days 5 and 6, which brought her to exactly 70% of the trail. On day 7 she walked two-thirds of the distance still remaining, and she finished with 18 km on day 8.
How long is the trail?
solution: Work back from the end. After day 6, 30% of the trail remained. Day 7 covered two-thirds of that (20%), so day 8's 18 km is the last 10%: the trail is 180 km. Check: 40% is 72 km (day 4 must have been 72 - 62 = 10 km), and 72 + 27 + 27 = 126 km = 70%.

text:
A school will varnish the floors of 12 classrooms, using the same type of varnish throughout. The caretaker has found these tin prices and worked out how much each type needs per room:

| varnish | 0.5 litre | 1 litre | 2.5 litres | needed per room |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P | €4.00 | €7.00 | €15.00 | 0.9 litres |
| Q | €3.00 | €6.00 | €16.00 | 0.75 litres |
| R | not sold | €5.00 | €11.00 | 1.1 litres |
| S | €2.50 | not sold | €12.00 | 0.8 litres |

What is the least the school can spend?
solution: Total needed for 12 rooms: P 10.8 L, Q 9 L, R 13.2 L, S 9.6 L. Cheapest buys: P 4 x 2.5 L + 1 L = €67; Q 9 x 1 L (or 18 x 0.5 L) = €54; R 5 x 2.5 L + 1 L = €60; S 4 x 2.5 L = 10 L for €48. S is cheapest at €48 even though R has the lowest price per litre in big tins.

text:
Many teenagers stay on social media late into the night, and those who do sleep, on average, an hour less than their classmates. Sleep is when the brain recovers from the day, and shortened sleep is known to affect mood. Brain scans show that teenagers who regularly sleep under seven hours have less activity in areas that help to regulate emotion than teenagers who sleep longer.
Which one of the following can be drawn as a conclusion from the passage above?
options: There may be a link between heavy late-night social media use and mood problems in teenagers.
Social media is the main cause of depression in teenagers.
Teenagers cannot tell online friends from real ones.
The structure of the brain is fixed at birth.
Phones should be banned for everyone under 16.
solution: The passage connects late-night use to less sleep, and less sleep to weaker emotion regulation, so a link between them is possible. The evidence is indirect and cautious, so it cannot show social media is the main cause of depression, says nothing about telling friends apart, suggests the brain responds to habits rather than being fixed, and recommends no ban.

text: Andreas Vesalius, author of De humani corporis fabrica (1543), is famous for
options: discovering the circulation of the blood.
accurate, detailed descriptions of human anatomy based on dissection.
being the first to see bacteria.
solution: Vesalius, who taught at Padua, dissected human bodies himself and corrected many errors handed down from Galen, founding modern anatomy. William Harvey described the circulation in 1628, Jenner developed vaccination, and van Leeuwenhoek first saw bacteria with his own microscopes.

text: What does the letter A stand for in NATO?
solution: NATO is the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, founded by the North Atlantic Treaty signed in Washington in 1949. Its members commit to collective defence: an attack on one is treated as an attack on all.

text: The painters Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque are associated with which art movement?
solution: Picasso and Braque developed Cubism around 1907-1914, showing objects from several viewpoints at once as geometric shapes. Futurism was an Italian movement led by Marinetti, Surrealism was led by Breton and Dalí, Impressionism by Monet and Renoir, and the Baroque belongs to the 17th century.

text: Who invented the World Wide Web in 1989 while working at CERN?
solution: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web at CERN, near Geneva, in 1989, and wrote the first web browser and server. Gates and Jobs founded Microsoft and Apple, Turing laid the foundations of computer science, and Marconi pioneered radio.

text: After a person drinks a large amount of water, which structure detects that their blood has become more dilute, and which structure responds by releasing less ADH?
options: the pituitary gland, then the hypothalamus
the hypothalamus, then the pituitary gland
solution: Osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect the fall in the concentration of the blood. The hypothalamus then signals the posterior pituitary gland, which releases less ADH, so the kidneys reabsorb less water and make more, dilute urine. The kidney is the target of ADH, not the detector.

text: Which statement about asexual reproduction is correct?
options: It produces offspring genetically identical to the parent, unless a mutation occurs.
It uses meiosis to make gametes.
It produces more genetic variation than sexual reproduction.
solution: Asexual reproduction uses mitosis (or binary fission) from a single parent, so the offspring are clones; only mutations make them differ. Gametes, meiosis and two parents belong to sexual reproduction, which is the source of more variation. Many plants, fungi and some animals reproduce asexually too.

text:
The template strand of a short gene reads TAC GGC ATT. A mutation replaces the fifth base of this template, G, with A.
Which mRNA is transcribed from the mutated template?
solution: The mutated template is TAC GAC ATT. The mRNA pairs with it base by base, with U for A: AUG CUG UAA. AUG CCG UAA is the mRNA from the original template; anything with T is DNA; UAC GAC AUU just copies the template with U; CAG puts the change in the wrong place.

text:
A species of fish lives in very cold water, and its cell membranes stay fluid at that temperature.
Compared with a related fish from warm water, what would you expect to find more of in the phospholipids of its membranes?
options: ionic bonds between the phosphate heads
unsaturated fatty acid tails, with C=C double bonds
solution: Each C=C double bond puts a kink in a fatty acid tail, so the tails cannot pack tightly together, and the membrane stays fluid in the cold. Saturated, straight tails pack closely and would make the membrane stiffen. Peptide bonds are in proteins, not phospholipids.

text:
Which of the following are found in an influenza virus particle?
1 RNA
2 DNA
3 phospholipids
4 proteins
solution: Influenza is an RNA virus: its genes are RNA, with no DNA. Its genome sits in a protein capsid, wrapped in an envelope of phospholipid taken from the host cell's membrane, studded with viral proteins. So 1, 3 and 4.

text:
Which features make an impulse cross a synapse in one direction only?
1 Neurotransmitter is stored in vesicles only in the presynaptic knob.
2 Receptors for the neurotransmitter are found only on the postsynaptic membrane.
3 The axon is covered by a myelin sheath.
solution: Transmitter can only be released from the presynaptic side, where the vesicles are, and it can only act where its receptors are, on the postsynaptic side. Myelin speeds up conduction along the axon (saltatory conduction) but has nothing to do with direction at a synapse. 1 and 2 only.

text:
Which of the following can fuse with vesicles in a eukaryotic cell?
1 the cell surface membrane
2 the Golgi apparatus
3 lysosomes
solution: Secretory vesicles fuse with the cell surface membrane in exocytosis; vesicles from the rough ER fuse with the Golgi apparatus; and vesicles carrying engulfed material fuse with lysosomes so it can be digested. All three.

text:
A ring of DNA 4000 bp around is cut by one enzyme at three positions, numbered round the ring: 500, 1500 and 3200.
How long is each resulting piece?
solution: Three cuts in a circle make three pieces. From 500 to 1500 is 1000 bp; from 1500 to 3200 is 1700 bp; from 3200 round past the end (4000) back to 500 is 800 + 500 = 1300 bp. Check: 1000 + 1700 + 1300 = 4000. Treating the plasmid as a straight line gives four pieces, including separate 500 and 800 bp ends.

text: The valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle (the bicuspid valve) closes when:
options: the pressure in the aorta rises above the pressure in the left ventricle.
the pressure in the left ventricle rises above the pressure in the left atrium.
the pressure in the left atrium rises above the pressure in the left ventricle.
solution: A valve is pushed shut when the pressure behind it rises above the pressure in front. As the left ventricle starts to contract, its pressure exceeds the atrium's and the bicuspid valve snaps shut, stopping backflow. Higher atrial pressure opens it; aortic pressure controls the aortic valve, not this one.

text: On the rough endoplasmic reticulum, what is attached to the outer surface of the membrane, and what passes through the membrane into the lumen?
options: outer surface: DNA; into the lumen: mRNA
outer surface: a polypeptide; into the lumen: ribosomes
outer surface: tRNA; into the lumen: glucose
outer surface: ribosomes; into the lumen: the growing polypeptide
outer surface: chromosomes; into the lumen: phospholipids
solution: The ribosomes on the outside of the rough ER give it its 'rough' look. As they translate mRNA, the new polypeptide is threaded through the membrane into the lumen, where it folds and is modified before travelling to the Golgi in vesicles. DNA and chromosomes never leave the nucleus.

text:
Which row correctly describes cell P as a typical animal cell and cell Q as a typical yeast cell?

| | cell P | cell Q |
|---|---|---|
| row 1 | has a cell wall | has centrioles |
| row 2 | has chloroplasts | has 70S ribosomes only |
| row 3 | stores starch | has no nucleus |
| row 4 | has no mitochondria | has a cell wall containing chitin |
| row 5 | has centrioles | has a cell wall containing chitin |
solution: Animal cells have centrioles and no wall; yeast is a fungus, a eukaryote with a nucleus, 80S ribosomes and a wall containing chitin. Animal cells have mitochondria, store glycogen not starch, and have no chloroplasts. Row 5.

text:
In aerobic respiration, glucose is broken down to substance P in the cytoplasm. P then enters a mitochondrion, where it is converted into substance Q, releasing carbon dioxide, and Q enters the Krebs cycle.
Which option identifies P and Q and the site where P becomes Q?
options: P = pyruvate; Q = acetyl coenzyme A; site = mitochondrial matrix
P = acetyl coenzyme A; Q = pyruvate; site = cytoplasm
P = lactate; Q = ethanol; site = cytoplasm
P = pyruvate; Q = lactate; site = cristae
P = glucose phosphate; Q = citrate; site = stroma
solution: Glycolysis turns glucose into pyruvate in the cytoplasm. In the link reaction, in the mitochondrial matrix, pyruvate loses carbon dioxide and joins coenzyme A to become acetyl coenzyme A, which feeds the Krebs cycle. Lactate and ethanol are the products of fermentation when oxygen is short.

text: What is the pH of 0.001 mol/L nitric acid, a strong acid?
solution: Nitric acid dissociates completely, so \([\mathrm{H^+}] = 0.001 = 10^{-3}\) mol/L and pH = \(-\log_{10}(10^{-3}) = 3\). A pH of -3 forgets the minus sign in the definition; 11 is the pH of a base of that concentration.

text:
Iron filings (3.36 g) are added to excess copper(II) sulfate solution:
\(\mathrm{Fe + CuSO_4 \rightarrow FeSO_4 + Cu}\)
The copper formed is filtered off, dried and weighed: 2.29 g.
What is the percentage yield, approximately?
[Relative atomic masses: Fe = 56; Cu = 63.5]
solution: 3.36 g of iron is 3.36/56 = 0.060 mol, and the reaction is 1 : 1, so at most 0.060 mol of copper forms: 0.060 x 63.5 = 3.81 g. Yield = 2.29/3.81 x 100, about 60%. 68% compares the masses of copper and iron directly (2.29/3.36).

text:
A small button battery runs on the reaction:
\(\mathrm{Zn + Ag_2O \rightarrow ZnO + 2Ag}\)
Which option gives the change in oxidation number of zinc and of silver during discharge?
solution: Zinc metal is 0 and in ZnO it is +2: oxidised. In \(\mathrm{Ag_2O}\), two silvers balance one oxygen at -2, so each is +1, and silver metal is 0: reduced. Electrons lost by zinc (2) equal electrons gained by the two silvers (1 each).

text:
Ethanol can be converted into each of these compounds:
ethene, ethanal, ethanoic acid, ethyl ethanoate, chloroethane
Which one is made by removing a molecule of water from ethanol (dehydration)?
solution: \(\mathrm{C_2H_5OH \rightarrow C_2H_4 + H_2O}\): taking H and OH from neighbouring carbons leaves a C=C double bond, ethene. Ethanal and ethanoic acid come from oxidising ethanol, ethyl ethanoate from esterification with ethanoic acid, and chloroethane from substituting the OH.

text:
Excess marble chips are added to 50 \(\mathrm{cm^3}\) of 1.0 mol/L hydrochloric acid at 25 °C, and the carbon dioxide given off is collected until the reaction stops. The experiment is repeated with the same mass of marble, now powdered, and everything else the same.
What happens to the rate of reaction (R) and the total volume of carbon dioxide (V)?
options: R: no change; V: no change
solution: Powder has a much larger surface area, so acid particles collide with the solid more often and the rate rises. The marble is in excess both times, so the acid is the limiting reagent, and the same amount of acid gives the same total volume of gas.

text: Which atomic number belongs to an atom whose ground-state electron configuration ends in \(3p^2\)?
solution: Count: \(1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2\) is 12 electrons, and \(3p^2\) adds two more: 14, silicon. Atomic number 6 (carbon) ends in \(2p^2\), the same pattern one shell lower; 13 ends in \(3p^1\) and 16 in \(3p^4\).

text:
What is the smallest volume of 0.50 mol/L sulfuric acid that will neutralise 4.0 g of sodium hydroxide?
\(\mathrm{H_2SO_4 + 2NaOH \rightarrow Na_2SO_4 + 2H_2O}\)
[\(M_r\) of NaOH = 40]
solution: 4.0 g of NaOH is 0.10 mol. Each \(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}\) neutralises two NaOH, so 0.050 mol of acid is needed. Volume = 0.050/0.50 = 0.10 L = 100 cm3. Ignoring the 1 : 2 ratio gives 200 cm3.

text:
Classify these oxides as acidic, amphoteric (reacting with both acids and alkalis) or basic:
\(\mathrm{Na_2O} \quad \mathrm{SO_3} \quad \mathrm{ZnO} \quad \mathrm{CO_2} \quad \mathrm{CaO} \quad \mathrm{P_4O_{10}} \quad \mathrm{Al_2O_3}\)
How many are in each group?
solution: Oxides of non-metals are acidic: \(\mathrm{SO_3}\), \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) and \(\mathrm{P_4O_{10}}\) (3). Zinc oxide and aluminium oxide are the classic amphoteric oxides (2). Oxides of reactive metals are basic: \(\mathrm{Na_2O}\) and CaO (2).

text:
Consider these conversions:
primary alcohol → (process P) → aldehyde
alkene + steam → compound Y
ester + water → alcohol + compound Z
Which option correctly identifies P, Y and Z?
options: P: reduction; Y: alkane; Z: ketone
P: oxidation; Y: alkane; Z: carboxylic acid
P: reduction; Y: alcohol; Z: carboxylic acid
P: oxidation; Y: ether; Z: aldehyde
P: oxidation; Y: alcohol; Z: carboxylic acid
solution: Turning a primary alcohol into an aldehyde removes hydrogen: oxidation. Adding water across the C=C of an alkene (hydration) gives an alcohol. Hydrolysing an ester splits it back into the alcohol and the carboxylic acid it was made from.

text:
Which two of these molecules are polar?
\(\mathrm{CH_4} \quad \mathrm{HBr} \quad \mathrm{BF_3} \quad \mathrm{CHCl_3} \quad \mathrm{CO_2}\)
solution: HBr has one polar bond, so the molecule is polar. In trichloromethane one H replaces a Cl, so the bond dipoles no longer cancel. Methane (tetrahedral), \(\mathrm{BF_3}\) (trigonal planar) and \(\mathrm{CO_2}\) (linear) are symmetrical, and their bond dipoles cancel.

subject: Physics
text:
A 2.0 kg box is pulled across a level floor by a horizontal force of 14 N. The coefficient of kinetic friction between box and floor is 0.30.
What is the box's acceleration once it is moving?
[Take \(g = 10\ \text{N kg}^{-1}\).]
solution: Friction = \(\mu mg = 0.30 \times 2.0 \times 10 = 6.0\) N. Resultant force = 14 - 6.0 = 8.0 N, so \(a = F/m = 8.0/2.0 = 4.0\ \text{m/s}^2\). Ignoring friction gives 7.0.

subject: Mathematics
text: Find the line through (3, -4) that is perpendicular to \(2y - 5x = 7\).
solution: Rearranged, the given line is \(y = \tfrac{5}{2}x + \tfrac{7}{2}\), gradient \(\tfrac{5}{2}\), so the perpendicular gradient is \(-\tfrac{2}{5}\). Through (3, -4): \(5(y + 4) = -2(x - 3)\), giving \(2x + 5y = -14\). The first, fourth and fifth options pass through the point but have the wrong gradient.

subject: Mathematics
text:
Evaluate
\[\frac{6 \times 10^{4}}{\sqrt{9 \times 10^{-6}}} \times \left(2 \times 10^{-3}\right)^2\]
solution: \(\sqrt{9 \times 10^{-6}} = 3 \times 10^{-3}\), so the fraction is \(2 \times 10^{7}\). \((2 \times 10^{-3})^2 = 4 \times 10^{-6}\). Multiplying: \(8 \times 10^{1} = 80\).

subject: Mathematics
text:
Three cubes have edges of length \(a\), \(2a\) and \(3a\).
What is the total surface area of the three cubes?
solution: A cube of edge \(x\) has six faces of area \(x^2\), so \(6x^2\). Total: \(6(a^2 + 4a^2 + 9a^2) = 6 \times 14a^2 = 84a^2\). Doubling an edge multiplies the area by 4, not 2. (36 is the coefficient of the total VOLUME, \(a^3 + 8a^3 + 27a^3\).)

subject: Mathematics
text:
After a 25% price rise, a concert ticket costs €45.00.
What did it cost before the rise?
solution: The new price is 125% of the old one, so the old price is 45.00 / 1.25 = €36.00. Taking 25% off €45.00 (€33.75) is the trap: 25% of the new price is more than 25% of the old one.

subject: Physics
text:
A bar of material is attracted by the north pole of a bar magnet, and also by its south pole. No electric charges or currents are involved.
What could the bar be made of?
solution: Either pole of a magnet induces magnetism in unmagnetised iron, always with the opposite pole facing it, so iron is attracted by both. A magnetised bar would be repelled by one of the poles, which is the only real test for a magnet. Copper, aluminium and glass are not magnetic.
